insights.headline: She reads people's private records covertly at three life stages, and each time frames it as vigilance or grief rather than as the same act.
insights.explanation: She reads her mother's hidden journal for two years at ten (E1), reads two years of Jeremy's email at twenty-four (E2), and reads her mother's email to Roseanne as an adult (E4). Each instance gets a different justification -- hypervigilance origin, 'I just get uncomfortable when I don't know where people are mentally,' and 'somebody has to hold the whole picture' -- but the mechanism (secret access to someone's unfiltered interior, alone, at night or on the sly) is identical, and she never connects the three across the telling.

insights.would_predict: Relationships: Marriage and partnership -- if she and Nic move in together or marry, she will at some point access his phone, email, or messages without telling him, framed to herself as due diligence or care rather than surveillance.

insights.headline: She believes closeness is dangerous only once it becomes real, and she manufactures the ending herself in every account of romantic or peer bonding.
insights.explanation: With Jeremy she ends it three weeks before the lease signs, right after his sister says 'we feel like we already know you' (E2). With her cohort she leaves the group chat days after the moment she was most seen and praised (E5). With the duplex she names the same nervous-system read ('permanent... is going to be taken from you') while it is happening but still has not told Nic, keeping the same distance mechanism running even with full self-awareness (E5).

evidence.quote: I have this thing where the second something is real I get certain that it's going to be taken, and so I take it first. I leave before I'm left.
Anytime something becomes permanent my nervous system reads permanent as, this is the thing that's going to be taken from you.

insights.would_predict: Relationships: Marriage and partnership -- naming the pattern aloud to Nic will not, on its own, prevent a withdrawal behavior (silence, sudden 'boundary,' canceled plan) in the weeks immediately surrounding the house purchase closing.

insights.headline: She protects other people's dignity at direct cost to her own visibility, consistently and without collecting credit.
insights.explanation: She never told Kelsey about the journal, sparing her the burden of it (E1). She kept the RIF list airtight for eleven weeks, steering four people without ever breaking confidence, at the cost of her own health (E3). She sent anonymous money to Terrence's GoFundMe specifically so it would be 'from nobody' (E3). This is a genuine value pattern -- protection chosen even when it isolates or costs her -- distinct from her stated 'over-functioning' framing, which treats it purely as pathology.

evidence.quote: For eleven weeks I steered her. I steered like four people. Never said a word, never broke it, never — I mean, I was airtight.

insights.would_predict: Work and Career: Finances and stewardship -- she will decline credit or attribution for a financial or professional favor she does for a colleague or client at least once more, and will not mention it unless directly asked.

insights.headline: Her own bodily and financial facts are the flattest data in every story; other people's numbers are exact.
insights.explanation: She names Danielle's mortgage rate conversation, the RIF headcount (206/51), timing to the minute (10:40, fourteen minutes each), and her mother's exact PIN logic, but her own body appears only as clinical shorthand -- 'I got shingles at twenty-nine' (no lead-up, no sensation), 'sleeping four hours' (no felt account), and money going to or from her is either invisible (her own finances never appear) or symbolic (the $11,000 loan is her grandfather's, not hers). The single place her own body gets duration and repetition is compulsive activity -- swimming a mile nightly, reorganizing a closet till 2am -- never rest or symptom.

evidence.quote: I got shingles at twenty-nine. Twenty-nine!
Like sleeping four hours, in the pool at nine at night, cleaning the grout with a toothbrush at midnight

insights.would_predict: Health and Wellness: Physical health -- in a medical visit, she will underreport symptom severity or timeline compared to what a symptom log would show, and will describe a health issue primarily in terms of what tasks it disrupted.

insights.headline: After every moment of being truly seen or having done the hardest work, she drives alone at night rather than telling anyone what just happened.
insights.explanation: After the Denise confrontation lands and the room calls it the most vulnerable thing they'd heard all semester, she drives to Golden and sits by the Coors plant for ninety minutes (E5). After ending things with Jeremy, and during the eight days before, she drives to Idaho Springs and back at 11pm repeatedly (E2). After the last RIF conversation and Marcy's praise, she reorganizes a closet till 2am and drives to a 24-hour King Soopers (E3). The solitary night drive/errand is the release valve in three separate decades, always alone, always right after an interpersonal event that landed.

evidence.quote: I'd get in the car at eleven at night and drive up 70 to Idaho Springs and turn around and come back. Just — like ninety minutes. Radio off, usually.
I went out and got in my car and I drove to Golden and sat in the parking lot by the Coors plant for like an hour and a half. And I'm not totally sure why.

insights.would_predict: Health and Wellness: Rest and recreation -- she will report to a partner or friend that she needs 'alone time' or 'to drive' after a significant emotional event rather than seeking company, and will not disclose what triggered it.

insights.headline: She states she has become someone who asks directly for what she needs, but no experience shows her doing it with a person who could actually refuse her.
insights.explanation: She cites 'I will say to Nic, hey, I need twenty minutes' (E3) as evidence of growth, and calls the ability to name her pattern aloud 'the whole difference' (E5). Yet across five accounts the only direct disclosures of need she narrates are either to a therapist/supervision setting (safe, paid, one-directional) or performed for an audience that then praises her for it (Denise's group). She still declines Nic's offer to attend appointments (E4), still hasn't told him about the duplex anxiety (E5), and still went off at Kelsey only after over a year of silent accumulation rather than an early direct ask.

evidence.quote: I haven't said any of it to Nic because he's so happy about the sunroom and I don't want to put that on him

insights.would_predict: Relationships: Communication and conflict -- in the next 12 months, a direct request for help from Nic will be preceded by weeks of unspoken accumulation and will surface as anger or a 'went off' moment rather than a calm ask.

insights.headline: Every account ends with an external verdict of her competence, delivered by an authority figure, immediately following her greatest private cost -- and she records the line verbatim each time.
insights.explanation: Her mother says 'the kitchen fairy came' after midnight reorganizing (E1). Marcy says 'you crushed it today, go home' right after 19 termination conversations (E3). The room says 'wow' after her four-second, textbook-perfect answer to Denise (E5). She quotes each verdict word for word but gives almost no space to what she wanted to hear instead, except once: 'I was waiting for her to say, what do you need. That's all. And she never did' (E4). That single named absence exposes what the other verdicts are standing in for.

evidence.quote: you crushed it today, go home
I was waiting for her to say, what do you need. That's all. And she never did.

insights.would_predict: Work and Career: Leadership and collaboration -- in her clinical training or future practice, she will feel most satisfied after a supervisor praises her performance under difficulty, and will not proactively ask a supervisor for support even when overwhelmed.

insights.headline: The fluent self-diagnosis that reads as growth in E5 is the same tool she used to end the relationship in E2 -- eloquence is functioning as an exit mechanism, not (only) insight.
insights.explanation: In E2, she delivers Jeremy an 'articulate speech' about needing to grow, and notes 'I said it so well... he didn't have anything to say back to it because how do you argue with somebody doing work on themselves.' In E5, she produces an equally polished four-second clinical formulation in response to Denise's confrontation ('I have a pretty deeply grooved pattern where I take the helper position because being the one who's known feels unsafe...') and the room responds with awe, not challenge -- then she leaves the group chat days later. Read alone, E5 looks like hard-won therapeutic fluency; read against E2, the fluency itself is the same maneuver that ended a relationship: producing insight so complete that no one can follow up or get closer.

evidence.quote: I was twenty-four and I delivered it like a closing argument and he didn't have anything to say back to it because how do you argue with somebody doing work on themselves.

insights.would_predict: Work and Career: Zone of genius at work -- as a therapist, she will occasionally produce a clinically fluent, complete-sounding interpretation of her own reaction mid-session with a client or supervisor that functions to end the line of inquiry rather than open it, and colleagues will rarely push back on it.

insights.headline: No experience contains her wanting something she does not already know how to get herself, or being surprised by receiving help.
insights.explanation: Across five accounts spanning ages 10 to 37, every want she names is either fulfilled by her own action (dinner started before the lawyer calls, mail forwarded, lists built, closets reorganized) or explicitly denied/unspoken (Kelsey's 'what do you need,' Nic's appointment offer declined, the group chat exit instead of asking for space). The corpus has clear room for an instance of accepted help -- a marriage, a mother's care, a decade of therapy, a cohort of 12 peers -- yet no scene shows her on the receiving end of unprompted care she did not manage or predict first.

So Thursday I'd come home and I'd have already started dinner.
